briefings.tldr: The "50-State Plan" is a strategic initiative to democratize AI by establishing high-performance computing infrastructure in every U.S. state through public-private partnerships, ensuring that AI literacy and research capabilities drive regional economic growth across all academic disciplines.
briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR**
The "50-State Plan" is a strategic initiative to democratize AI by establishing high-performance computing infrastructure in every U.S. state through public-private partnerships, ensuring that AI literacy and research capabilities drive regional economic growth across all academic disciplines.

## The "50-State Solution" and Public-Private Partnerships
* **The Florida Model as a Blueprint:** Chris Malachowsky (NVIDIA Co-founder) detailed the success of gifting a supercomputer to the University of Florida, which served as a catalyst for statewide AI literacy and a $200 million state investment in faculty.
* **NVIDIA’s Commitment:** To scale this nationwide, NVIDIA announced it will:
    * **Match Contributions:** Provide discounts to match donor contributions for university AI infrastructure.
    * **Software Access:** Provide its world-class software stack to universities for free.
    * **Priority Access:** Prioritize the delivery of advanced technology to support U.S. economic infrastructure.
* **Capitalizing on Philanthropy:** The model relies on "paying it forward," encouraging private benefactors in every state to fund hardware that serves as a regional economic engine rather than just an engineering tool.

## National Infrastructure and Regional Innovation
* **The National AI Research Resource (NAIRR):** Brian Stone (NSF) highlighted the NAIRR pilot, a federal-private partnership (including NVIDIA) that currently supports over 600 projects. 
    * **Scope of Research:** Interestingly, 60% of NAIRR projects are in non-AI fields like material science and geophysics, demonstrating that AI is now the primary tool for all scientific discovery.
* **Regional Innovation Engines:** The NSF’s "TIP" (Technology, Innovation, and Partnerships) directorate is focused on creating regional hubs that align with local economic needs, such as agriculture in the Midwest or power systems in the Carolinas.
* **Consortium Models:** States are moving away from "bespoke servers under desks" toward unified strategies:
    * **AI Tennessee:** A statewide consortium including technical colleges, community colleges, and four-year institutions to share expertise.
    * **Keystone AI (Pennsylvania):** A historic MOU signed by all seven R1 research institutions in the state to share resources and infrastructure.

## Transforming the Workforce and Curriculum
* **Universal AI Literacy:** Panelists emphasized that AI must be "the subject of learning and integrated into learning" across every department.
    * **The Humanities Gap:** Deborah Crawford (U of Tennessee) noted that the highest engagement for AI fellowships often comes from non-STEM faculty (Arts, Law, Social Sciences) seeking to understand how the technology reshapes their fields.
* **Community College Integration:** A major priority is ensuring AI access isn't limited to elite "R1" universities. 
    * **Democratization:** Success is defined by providing community colleges and minority-serving institutions with the same compute cycles as top-tier research centers to prevent a new digital divide.
* **The "Eds and Meds" Strategy:** Theresa Mayer (Carnegie Mellon) cited Pittsburgh’s transition from steel to a high-tech economy as a model for how university-led AI research can rebuild a region’s manufacturing base.

## Success Metrics for the Next Decade
* **Computation as a Utility:** Chris Malachowsky argued that computational resources must eventually be viewed as public infrastructure, similar to water or electricity.
* **Physical AI and Robotics:** The next frontier is "Sim-to-Real"—using AI to control physical systems, autonomous labs, and advanced manufacturing.
* **Economic Outcomes:** Success will be measured by:
    * **Placement Statistics:** Doubling or tripling student job placement rates.
    * **Research Funding:** Increasing the flow of federal and private research dollars into state economies.
    * **Startup Incubation:** Providing "near-term" compute access to university startups so they remain in-state rather than migrating to tech hubs.

> "The machine is really just a catalyst. It's a piece of iron. It's what you do with it that's kind of magical... The 50-state solution [ensures] every state has someone willing to promote their institutions on the same technological footing as the best in the world."
> — **Chris Malachowsky**, NVIDIA Co-founder

> "Within a few short years—or now—everybody is going to be an AI researcher in some way, because we will all use it. We have to embrace it and lean into it."
> — **Brian Stone**, Chief of Staff, National Science Foundation

> "Success is us shifting our thinking. AI is not 'this or that'—AI is a cross-cut. It is the engine for the future of our nation."
> — **Theresa Mayer**, VP for Research, Carnegie Mellon University

briefings.title: The Misleading Advice Every Entrepreneur Gets Wrong with Bill Gurley
briefings.tldr: Successful careers and high-growth ventures are built on the "30-year test" of long-term sustainability and the exploitation of network effects, often requiring a degree of "healthy self-delusion" to tackle challenges that more experienced leaders might find too daunting.
briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR**
Successful careers and high-growth ventures are built on the "30-year test" of long-term sustainability and the exploitation of network effects, often requiring a degree of "healthy self-delusion" to tackle challenges that more experienced leaders might find too daunting.

## Career Transitions and the "30-Year Test"
Bill Gurley highlights a specific heuristic he used to pivot from engineering at Compaq to Wall Street research, and finally to Venture Capital (VC).

*   **The 30-Year Question:** Periodically ask: "Do I want to be doing this for the next 30 years?" 
    *   If the work feels monotonous or the "corner office" path lacks personal fulfillment, a pivot is necessary.
    *   Gurley left Compaq when he realized his third project looked identical to his first two.
*   **The "Spare Time" Indicator:** Your true curiosity is revealed by what you do in your unpaid hours.
    *   While an engineer, Gurley spent his spare time reading about Wall Street and buying stocks, which signaled a need for a career change.
*   **Breadth vs. Detail:** Different roles suit different temperaments.
    *   **Service Roles:** VCs, lawyers, and consultants often favor diversity and breadth over ownership and deep technical detail.
    *   **Founders/CEOs:** These roles require people who want to be "in the weeds" and in control of a single, growing entity.

## Identifying and Scaling "Winners"
Reflecting on investments like Uber, Zillow, and OpenTable, Gurley identifies the specific patterns that lead to thousand-fold returns.

*   **Network Effects (Increasing Returns):** Gurley looks for businesses that become more valuable as they grow.
    *   **OpenTable Example:** When Gurley funded the company, it had only three restaurants. The bet was on the "network effect"—more restaurants attract more consumers, which in turn forces more restaurants to join.
*   **The Founder as Salesperson:** A founder’s primary job is selling, regardless of their technical background.
    *   They must sell to investors for capital, to candidates for recruiting, and to partners for business development.
*   **Go-to-Market (GTM) Advantage:** Successful startups find a unique, faster path to acquiring customers.
    *   This often involves leveraging new technologies (e.g., social media algorithms, AI) to gain awareness more efficiently than incumbents.

## The Psychology of Risk and Innovation
Gurley discusses the "delusional factor" necessary for outlier success and why many transformative founders are under the age of 25.

*   **The Necessity of Self-Delusion:** To "attack the hill" of a seemingly impossible problem, a leader needs a degree of self-delusion. 
    *   Most rational people would never start a company because the odds of failure are too high and the task is too daunting.
*   **The Naivety Advantage:** Younger leaders often succeed because they "don't know what they don't know."
    *   This lack of baggage allows them to ignore the "mental models" that often cause more experienced investors or leaders to say "no" to radical ideas.
*   **The "Edge" of Learning:** Venture capital is a "complex puzzle" because the edge of innovation is always moving (e.g., the shift from the early internet to the current AI-centric landscape).

## Missed Opportunities and Mental Models
Even legendary investors face massive failures in judgment based on rigid thinking.

*   **The Google Miss:** Gurley’s partnership at Benchmark had the opportunity to invest in Google when it had only 25 employees.
    *   **The Failure:** They "failed to lay chase" because the company didn't fit their existing mental models at the time.
    *   **The Consequence:** Legendary VCs John Doerr and Mike Moritz ended up closing the deal instead. Gurley cites this as the biggest mistake of his career.

***

**Notable Quotes**

> "I had this moment where I just stopped and reflected and asked myself the question, 'Is this what I want to be doing for the next 30 years?' ... It was provocative in my mind and very clear the answer [was no]." — **Bill Gurley**

> "What it is you do in your spare time might be that thing that you're ultimately most curious about." — **Bill Gurley**

> "There's a bit of self-delusion that may be required to attack the hill... the vast majority of people would never attack the hill because it's too daunting and everything looks impossible." — **Bill Gurley**

briefings.title: Vikings, Ragnar, Berserkers, Valhalla & the Warriors of the Viking Age | Lex Fridman Podcast #495
briefings.tldr: The Viking Age (793–1066 AD) was defined by unparalleled maritime mobility and a pragmatic warrior culture that reshaped Western civilization through "creative destruction," transitioning from terrifying raiders into the foundational architects of modern European states and the Byzantine Empire’s elite guard.
briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR**
The Viking Age (793–1066 AD) was defined by unparalleled maritime mobility and a pragmatic warrior culture that reshaped Western civilization through "creative destruction," transitioning from terrifying raiders into the foundational architects of modern European states and the Byzantine Empire’s elite guard.

## The Anatomy of Terror: Mobility and Psychological Warfare
* **The Lindisfarne Catalyst (793 AD):** The raid on the holy island of Lindisfarne shattered the medieval social contract. Monasteries were previously viewed as sacred "arks" of safety; the Vikings' refusal to respect religious taboos created a psychological "end of the world" sentiment across Christendom.
* **Technological Superiority:** 
    * **The Longship Advantage:** Viking ships featured a shallow draft of less than two feet, allowing them to sail up shallow rivers or be portaged by hand. 
    * **Speed Disparity:** While land-based Anglo-Saxon armies averaged 10–15 miles per day, Viking longships averaged 70–120 miles per day, allowing them to strike and retreat before an enemy could mobilize.
* **Calculated Sophistication:** Vikings were not "dumb brutes." They acted as merchants during peace to scout targets, studying the Christian calendar to strike on high holy days when churches were filled with wealth and high-value captives.

## The Viking Ethos: Pragmatism, Meritocracy, and Religion
* **Flat Hierarchy:** Unlike the rigid feudal systems of Europe, Viking warbands were meritocratic. When asked who their king was during the siege of Paris, the Vikings famously replied, "We have no king; we are all kings."
* **Hardened Culture:** Growing up at the limits of human survival near the Arctic Circle bred a culture where mercy was a secondary value. Strength was the primary currency, exemplified by the "Berserkers"—Odin’s warriors who fought with animalistic fury and total indifference to pain.
* **Cosmology of Doom:**
    * **Valhalla:** Viewed as a training ground where warriors fought and died daily to prepare for the final battle of Ragnarok.
    * **Inevitability of Chaos:** Unlike religions promising ultimate victory, Norse mythology posited that chaos would eventually defeat order. This fostered a "die well" mentality: since the end is fixed, bravery is the only meaningful choice.

## From Raiders to Rulers: "Creative Destruction"
* **The Norman Transition:** Historian Lars Brownworth describes the Viking impact as "creative destruction." By dismantling unwieldy, overextended empires (like Charlemagne’s), they cleared the ground for leaner, more vital states.
* **Rollo and Normandy:** In 911 AD, the Viking leader Rollo was granted land in northern France (Normandy) to serve as a buffer against other raiders. Within a single generation, these Vikings adopted the French language, Christianity, and names, yet retained a "Viking vitality" that led them to conquer England and Sicily.
* **Canute the Great:** A master state-builder who created the "North Sea Empire" (England, Denmark, and Norway). He stabilized England after decades of war and was recognized as a legitimate Christian peer by the Holy Roman Emperor.

## Global Reach: The Byzantine and American Frontiers
* **The Varangian Guard:** Swedish Vikings (Varangians) used the river systems of Russia (the Volga and Dnieper) to reach Constantinople. Impressed by their prowess, the Byzantine Emperor formed the Varangian Guard—an elite unit of Viking bodyguards renowned for being "loyal to the throne, if not the man sitting on it."
* **The Greenland "Scam":** Erik the Red, exiled for murder, founded the Greenland colony. He named it "Greenland" as a marketing ploy to attract settlers from overpopulated Iceland—the first major real estate scam in history.
* **North America (Vinland):** Leif Erikson reached the Americas approximately 500 years before Columbus. The settlement failed not due to lack of resources, but because of extreme distance from resupply and incessant resistance from native populations (the "Skraelings").

## Notable Quotes
> **Lars Brownworth:** "The Vikings were ultimately a pragmatic people who, if it worked, they would keep it... They disappear so quickly because they were so good at integrating."

> **Lars Brownworth:** "The Vikings hit this place [Lindisfarne], of all places you could hit, was the worst, the most terrifying kind of offense against medieval sensibilities... The dead were left as dung in the street."

> **Lars Brownworth:** "I like to call it creative destruction. By destroying the things they destroyed, they cleared the ground for something stronger to grow."

> **Lex Fridman (quoting the Volsunga Saga):** "Fear not death for the hour of your doom is set and none may escape it... Better to fight and fall than to live without hope."

briefings.title: What's God got to do with it? The case for faith in an age of AI
briefings.tldr: Faith communities represent over 80% of the global population, making them essential partners for addressing global challenges in climate, economics, and AI by grounding technical solutions in long-standing moral frameworks and human-centric values.
briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR** (1-2 sentences): Faith communities represent over 80% of the global population, making them essential partners for addressing global challenges in climate, economics, and AI by grounding technical solutions in long-standing moral frameworks and human-centric values.

## The Strategic Necessity of Engaging Faith
* **Massive Global Scale:** Approximately 80-85% of the world’s population identifies with a religion or faith tradition. To achieve goals in finance, climate, or technology, global leaders must know how to cooperate with these massive communities.
* **Reuniting Commerce and Values:** Historically, commerce and faith were deeply interlinked. Gopal Patel (FutureFaith) notes that they have become "delinked," and the goal is to reintroduce spiritual and moral considerations into economic and technical systems.
* **Mitigating Polarization:** By normalizing faith in professional and global contexts, leaders can prevent religion from being "co-opted by the extremes," which often leads to division and conflict.
* **Institutional Infrastructure:** Faith organizations possess vast, existing infrastructure—including hospitals, schools, and financial networks—that can be mobilized for the common good.

## Building a "Moral Economy"
* **Addressing Wealth Inequality:** The current economic system is failing many and causing environmental damage. The Council explores what a "moral economy" looks like—one that serves both people and the planet rather than rewarding greed.
* **Equitable Resource Distribution:** Drawing on Gandhi’s teaching that there is enough for "need but not for greed," faith leaders advocate for systems where capital flows toward human flourishing rather than simple accumulation.
* **The "Toolbox" Approach:** Soulaima Gourani (Happioh) explains that the Council is developing a "toolbox" for leaders and boards to ensure their policies and technologies are aligned with universal faith-based ethics.

## Environmental Stewardship and Climate Action
* **Depoliticizing Climate Language:** Because the phrase "climate change" has become politically charged and alienating, faith leaders aim to use language rooted in values and self-interest to mobilize the majority.
* **Translating Ancient Wisdom:** Every major religion has roots in nature (mountains, deserts, forests). The challenge is translating that 2,000-year-old wisdom into a modern urban context (e.g., London or Nairobi) to address the current crisis.
* **A Legacy of Leadership:** Faith groups have spent decades working on biodiversity and conservation; the Council seeks to catalyze this momentum through partnerships with the private sector.

## The Human Side of Artificial Intelligence
* **Research Acceleration:** Soulaima Gourani highlights that AI can compress 10 years of rare disease research into 10 days, offering immense potential for human longevity and healthcare.
* **The Soul vs. The Algorithm:** While AI can mimic personality, it lacks an "inner life" or soul. Faith provides a necessary framework for navigating the "human fallout" of AI, such as the grief and loss of identity associated with mass job displacement.
* **Guarding Against Misuse:** Tech leaders are increasingly open about their faith to ensure they build products that improve human lives rather than facilitating "evil" purposes, such as surveillance or social isolation.
* **Non-Transactional Relationships:** While AI can provide "all-knowing" answers, Gopal Patel argues it cannot replace the "revelation, surrender, and devotion" found in a spiritual relationship, which evolves as a human grows in consciousness.

## Advice for Global Leaders
* **Challenge Modern Assumptions:** Many global systems are built on Judeo-Christian assumptions that may no longer work or may never have worked in certain parts of the world.
* **Embrace Change:** Using Hindu philosophy, Patel suggests that when a system is "breaking," it is often a sign that something "new and beautiful" is coming. Leaders should not fear the end of old systems but work to usher in the new based on spirit and values.

> "There are two forces that have shaped the history of the world, and those are commerce and faith. Historically those were deeply interlinked with each other, and we live in a time now where they're increasingly delinked."
> — **Gopal Patel**, Co-Founder and President, FutureFaith

> "Faith is a normal thing, faith is something that most of us have, and if we don't use it in a healthy way... it will be co-opted by the extremes and that will cause further division."
> — **Gopal Patel**, Co-Founder and President, FutureFaith

> "Money has no soul, right? It's just a tool. You shouldn't be a slave of money... I think it's both making sure that there is enough for everyone, but also understanding that faith communities have an issue with the traditional financing industries."
> — **Soulaima Gourani**, Co-Founder and CEO, Happioh

> "We're not here to say that everyone needs to believe in God... We’re here to say that these wisdom traditions have been around for thousands of years... how do you harness that collective wisdom and infrastructure for the common good?"
> — **Gopal Patel**, Co-Founder and President, FutureFaith

briefings.title: What's Going on in Private Credit?
briefings.tldr: The private credit market, specifically direct lending, is entering a period of disillusionment as the long-term tailwinds of low interest rates and undisciplined underwriting collide with AI-driven disruption in the software sector and retail redemption pressures.
briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR**
The private credit market, specifically direct lending, is entering a period of disillusionment as the long-term tailwinds of low interest rates and undisciplined underwriting collide with AI-driven disruption in the software sector and retail redemption pressures.

## The Evolution of the Credit Sector
* **Historical Chronology:** Howard Marks (Co-Chairman, Oaktree Capital) outlines a 50-year progression from the acceptance of high-yield debt in the 1970s to the current marketing of direct lending to retail investors.
    * **1970s-80s:** Michael Milken popularized non-investment grade debt; the birth of Leveraged Buyouts (LBOs).
    * **1990s-2000s:** Growth of broadly syndicated loans, securitizations (CLOs), and "alternative investments" after the tech bubble.
    * **2010s-2020s:** Post-GFC regulation forced banks to retreat, creating a vacuum filled by non-bank "direct lending" to mid-market PE-sponsored companies.
* **Market Scale:** The private credit sector has ballooned from roughly $150 billion 20 years ago to approximately $2 trillion today.
* **Risk vs. Volatility:** Marks warns that the lack of price volatility in private loans—due to the absence of a public market—has been misinterpreted as a lack of credit risk. 

## The Anatomy of a Credit Bubble
* **The "New Thing" Trap:** Novel investment forms often escape skepticism because they are untested. Early success fuels envy, leading latecomers (the "imitators" and "idiots") to lower standards to deploy capital.
* **The Quality Erosion:** Hundreds of firms entered direct lending post-GFC without experiencing a full credit cycle. This influx of capital forced lenders to compete by accepting:
    * Lower yields and narrower spreads.
    * Reduced safety and "covenant-lite" loan documents.
    * Higher debt levels and "ARR loans" (based on revenue rather than profit).
* **The Role of Liquidity Mismatches:** Drawing parallels to 1929, Marks cites three primary bubble drivers: selling to unsuitable investors, providing heavy leverage, and the mismatch between illiquid assets and short-term redemption expectations.

## The Software Debt Crisis and AI Disruption
* **Concentration Risk:** Software debt now represents a massive portion of credit markets, specifically 20-30% of direct lending (compared to only 4-5% of the high-yield bond market).
* **The AI Tipping Point:** In late 2025 and early 2026, the release of powerful AI coding models (such as those from Anthropic) disrupted the "moat" thesis of the software industry, which previously relied on high-cost human programming and recurring subscription revenue.
* **Sentiment Shift:** As equity cushions for software companies evaporated due to AI disruption, the credit market faced a "cognitive tipping point" in February 2026.
    * **Redemption Pressures:** Investors in semi-liquid Business Development Companies (BDCs) began requesting withdrawals, leading to redemption limits and skepticism regarding Net Asset Values (NAVs).

## The End of the "Sea Change" Era
* **The Interest Rate Tailwind:** Private equity and direct lending matured during a 40-year period (1980-2021) of secularly declining interest rates, which boosted asset values and lowered borrowing costs.
* **The New Reality:** The 400-500 basis point rate hike starting in 2022 has "thrown sand in the gears."
    * **Refinancing Challenges:** Portfolio companies are struggling with lower coverage ratios (earnings vs. interest expense).
    * **Lower Returns:** MSCI estimates that U.S. PE funds saw annualized returns of only 5.8% between 2022 and Q3 2025, significantly trailing the S&P 500's 11.6%.
* **Oaktree’s Positioning:** Marks emphasizes that Oaktree maintained discipline by limiting direct lending to 20% of its performing credit assets and keeping software exposure "extremely small" relative to peers.

> "What the wise man does in the beginning, the fool does in the end." 
> — **Howard Marks**, quoting a classic investment adage

> "In the last several years, a lot of private equity companies have been saddled with capital structures that didn't anticipate a 400-basis-point increase in interest rates." 
> — **Bruce Karsh**, Co-Chairman and CIO, Oaktree Capital

> "The enduring lesson is not that booms can be prevented or that busts can be fully averted. It is that we need to remember how easily we forget. The antidote to irrational exuberance is not regulation by itself... but humility." 
> — **Howard Marks**

> "Today, investors are not discriminating between the potential winners and losers in the software space, and the entire sector is under pressure. The disruptions in headlines are largely flow- and sentiment-driven rather than the result of credit deterioration." 
> — **Armen Panossian, Bob O’Leary, and Craig Wiele**, Oaktree Internal Memo extract

briefings.title: Why The OpenAI Legal Battle Could Redefine The Future Of Artificial Intelligence
briefings.tldr: Elon Musk’s $134 billion lawsuit against OpenAI, set for trial in late April, represents a fundamental clash over whether the future of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) should remain a nonprofit public good or a high-capital for-profit enterprise.
briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR**
Elon Musk’s $134 billion lawsuit against OpenAI, set for trial in late April, represents a fundamental clash over whether the future of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) should remain a nonprofit public good or a high-capital for-profit enterprise.

## The Musk vs. OpenAI Legal Battle
* **Trial Timeline:** Jury selection is scheduled to begin on April 27th, marking a critical escalation in the feud between Elon Musk and Sam Altman.
* **Core Allegations:** Musk claims Altman and OpenAI leadership "unjustly enriched" themselves by transitioning from a nonprofit to a for-profit structure, violating the company's founding mission.
* **OpenAI’s Counter-Defense:** Executives allege Musk’s legal action is motivated by "ego" and bitterness over his failed 2018 attempt to take over the company and merge it with Tesla.
* **Financial Remedies:** While the suit seeks $134 billion, Musk's legal team recently clarified that he is not seeking personal gain; instead, he requests that damages be awarded to OpenAI’s nonprofit foundation to restore its original mission.

## IPO Pressures and Market Competition
* **SpaceX and xAI Merger:** Elon Musk’s companies, SpaceX and xAI, reportedly filed confidentially to go public on April 1st, with a potential IPO expected as early as June.
* **OpenAI’s Public Aspirations:** OpenAI is rushing toward its own IPO, potentially later this year. Phoebe Liu notes that if Musk succeeds in forcing a reversion to a nonprofit structure, it would be "much harder to accomplish" once the company is publicly traded.
* **The "Capital Race":** Current AI leaders (OpenAI, Anthropic) are winning primarily because they have the most capital.
    * **Burn Rate:** These companies are generating billions in revenue but losing even more due to the massive computing costs required to train and run models.
    * **Funding Dependency:** OpenAI likely needs the public markets’ equity and debt funding to continue its current trajectory.

## Allegations of Anti-Competitive Behavior
* **Regulatory Requests:** OpenAI has sent letters to officials in California and Delaware requesting investigations into Musk for "anti-competitive behavior" ahead of the trial.
* **The Zuckerberg Connection:** OpenAI alleges that Musk and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg have coordinated "opposition research" and attacks against Sam Altman to undermine OpenAI’s market position.
* **Failed Smear Campaigns:** Reports suggest that extensive opposition research into Altman’s conduct—aimed at painting him as prioritizing profit over safety—has yielded "close to nothing" that could be substantiated or published.

## The Future of AGI Development
* **Nonprofit vs. For-Profit Trajectory:** 
    * A nonprofit OpenAI would be obligated to release models publicly, potentially slowing the current "AI revolution" but democratizing access.
    * A for-profit OpenAI continues to keep its most powerful models closed to maximize revenue and attract the billions in investment needed to compete with Google’s DeepMind.
* **Succession Planning:** Amid the turmoil, Sam Altman has reportedly joked about an "AI CEO" taking over OpenAI in the future, signaling that he may not intend to lead the company indefinitely after it goes public.

> "The companies that are leading the AI race right now are the companies that have the most capital... [OpenAI is] making billions of dollars in revenue per month and losing even more." — Phoebe Liu

> "Elon did not want any of the 134 billion to be for his personal gain. He wanted to put it in the nonprofit's bank... that dismantles a lot of the claims that he just wants this to be rich." — Phoebe Liu

> "If [OpenAI reverts to a nonprofit], that will change how the world is thinking about AI because this is the most well-capitalized for-profit now AI company in the world." — Phoebe Liu
